synonyms: ["Shoulder Tumors", "Growth In The Shoulder", "Masses In The Shoulder Area", "Tumors In The Shoulder Region"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, shoulder swelling is typically a symptom of an underlying condition such as bursitis, tendinitis, rotator cuff injury, arthritis, or infection. It may be accompanied by pain, stiffness, and reduced range of motion. Diagnosis often involves physical examination and imaging like ultrasound or MRI to identify fluid accumulation, inflammation, or structural damage. Treatment targets the specific cause - anti-inflammatories for bursitis, physical therapy for tendon issues, or antibiotics for infection.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments include rest, ice or heat application, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and corticosteroid injections to reduce pain and swelling. Physical therapy is commonly prescribed to restore mobility and strengthen supporting muscles. In cases of infection, antibiotics are necessary, and for severe structural damage or persistent symptoms, surgical options like arthroscopy may be considered.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the shoulder is a crossroads where several major channels pass - the Large Intestine, Small Intestine, Triple Burner, and Gallbladder meridians all traverse this area. When Qi and Blood flow smoothly, the shoulder stays supple and free of swelling. But when external pathogens like Wind, Cold, Damp, or Heat invade, or when internal imbalances disrupt circulation, the channels become blocked, fluids accumulate, and swelling appears.
The organ systems most involved are the Liver, which governs the sinews and ensures smooth Qi flow; the Spleen, which manages fluids and nourishes muscles; and the Kidney, which supports bones and overall vitality. A Spleen weakened by poor diet or fatigue may fail to transform fluids, leading to damp accumulation and a heavy, puffy swelling. Liver Qi stagnation - often from stress or frustration - can cause blood to congeal locally, producing a fixed, stabbing pain. When Kidney and Liver Yin are depleted, the joint loses its lubrication, and a chronic, dry swelling with stiffness sets in.
This is why the same Western diagnosis of shoulder swelling can have completely different TCM causes. A young athlete with a hot, red, swollen shoulder after an intense workout in humid weather likely has Damp-Heat. An older person with a dull, cold swelling that worsens in winter may have a Wind-Cold-Damp invasion superimposed on Qi and Blood Deficiency. By reading the quality of the swelling, the tongue, and the pulse, a TCM practitioner identifies the pattern and treats not just the swelling but the underlying susceptibility.
classical_quote: 「风寒湿三气杂至，合而为痹也。其风气胜者为行痹，寒气胜者为痛痹，湿气胜者为着痹也。」
classical_translation: "When the three Qi of Wind, Cold, and Dampness arrive together, they combine to form Bi syndrome. When Wind prevails, it is a moving Bi; when Cold prevails, it is a painful Bi; when Dampness prevails, it is a fixed Bi."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what the swelling feels like and what makes it better or worse. The quality of the pain, the presence of heat or cold, and how the shoulder reacts to weather and rest are the first clues that point toward one pattern rather than another.
If the shoulder feels heavy, stiff, and cold, and the pain worsens in damp or chilly weather, the pattern is likely Wind-Cold-Damp obstruction. The tongue usually has a white greasy coating, and the pulse feels tight or floating. This pattern often starts after exposure to cold drafts or wet conditions.
When the joint is visibly red, hot, and intensely painful with a sensation of burning, Damp-Heat is suspected. The tongue coating will be thick and yellow, and the pulse rapid and slippery. This acute, inflamed presentation is quite different from the cold, sluggish stiffness of the previous pattern.
If the swelling is accompanied by a fixed, stabbing pain that is worse at night, Blood Stagnation is the key pattern. There may be a history of old injury, and the tongue often appears dark or purplish with stasis spots. The pulse feels wiry or choppy, reflecting obstructed flow.
In long-standing cases where the swelling is mild but persistent, with a dull ache, fatigue, and limited range of motion that worsens after exertion, the root is often Qi and Blood Deficiency. The tongue is pale and the pulse is weak or thin. This pattern reflects a body too depleted to properly nourish and repair the sinews.
For older individuals or those with a constitutional weakness, chronic shoulder swelling may come with lower back and knee soreness, tinnitus, night sweats, and a feeling of heat in the palms and soles. This points to Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency. The tongue is red with little coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid.

patterns.why_this_happens: Wind, Cold, and Dampness are external pathogens that invade the body when your defenses are low, often after exposure to cold, damp weather or wearing wet clothes. They lodge in the shoulder channels, where Cold contracts and tightens the tissues, while Dampness causes fluid to accumulate, leading to swelling and a heavy sensation. The combined obstruction of Qi and Blood flow creates pain and stiffness that worsens in cold or damp conditions and improves with warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, slightly swollen with teeth marks, white greasy coating. Pulse: wiry and tight (弦紧, xián jǐn), slow (迟, chí) or soggy (濡, rú).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind, Cold, and Dampness are the very pathogens that obstruct the shoulder channels in this pattern. Cold and damp weather, drafts, and cold foods introduce more of these pathogens, worsening the stagnation and swelling. Warmth, gentle movement, and warm foods help disperse Cold, dry Dampness, and keep Qi and Blood flowing smoothly, reducing pain and swelling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the shoulder warm with a scarf or heating pad, especially in cold or damp weather. Gentle range-of-motion exercises help move Qi and prevent stagnation, but avoid overexertion. Eat warm, cooked foods and avoid raw, cold, or greasy items that can worsen internal dampness. Moxibustion on the shoulder area can provide deep warmth to dispel cold and damp.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Dampness and Heat combine and invade the shoulder channels, they create a heavy, hot, and swollen obstruction. Dampness causes the tissues to swell and feel heavy, while Heat brings redness, burning pain, and inflammation. The stuck Qi and Blood in the shoulder joint produce the characteristic red, hot, swollen, and acutely painful shoulder that feels worse with warmth and better with cold.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is a combination of excess moisture and heat in the body. Hot weather, spicy food, and alcohol add more heat, while greasy food and humidity increase dampness, making the shoulder more swollen and painful. Stress stirs up Liver Qi, which can generate more heat. Cool compresses, a dry environment, and cooling foods directly counteract the heat and dampness, while gentle movement helps Qi flow and prevents stagnation without overstraining the joint.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sweet foods that create Damp-Heat. Focus on cooling, damp-draining foods like barley, mung beans, cucumber, and bitter greens. Drink plenty of water. Rest the shoulder during acute flare-ups, but once the heat subsides, gentle range-of-motion exercises help prevent stiffness.

patterns.why_this_happens: When an old shoulder injury does not heal properly, or when long-standing Bi syndrome obstructs the channels, blood flow can become stuck in the local collaterals. This stagnant blood forms a fixed, hard swelling that presses on the tissues, causing a sharp, stabbing pain that refuses to move. Because blood stagnation deepens when the body is still and cold, the swelling and pain typically worsen at night and feel worse with pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with possible stasis spots; sublingual veins distended and dark. Pulse: choppy (涩, Sè), rough and uneven, or wiry (弦, Xián) if Qi stagnation is also present.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis is like a traffic jam in the vessels-movement and warmth help push blood through, while cold and stillness congeal it further. Gentle exercise and heat open the channels and encourage smooth flow, easing swelling and pain. Stress tightens Qi, which worsens the stagnation, so calming the mind and avoiding heavy foods that dampen circulation are crucial.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, black vinegar, and dark leafy greens. Avoid cold, raw foods and greasy meals that can congeal blood. Gentle daily movement, such as stretching and tai chi, helps prevent stagnation. Apply warm compresses to the shoulder to encourage circulation.

patterns.worse_with: Overwork or prolonged fatigue, Cold, damp, or rainy weather, Eating cold or raw foods, Insufficient sleep, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Rest and adequate sleep, Applying heat (warm compress or moxibustion), Warm foods and drinks, Gentle movement, stretching, or Tai Chi
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's Qi and Blood are chronically low, the sinews and channels in the shoulder lose their nourishment. The Spleen, which governs muscles and limbs, fails to transport fluids properly, leading to a lingering, mild swelling that is soft rather than firm. Because Blood is the substance that anchors the mind and soothes pain, the dull ache often worsens at night when Blood naturally returns to the Liver and leaves the channels temporarily emptier.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or show teeth marks on the edges, with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine, weak, and thready.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are the body's fundamental fuel and moisture. When they are deficient, every tissue becomes undernourished, and the shoulder's sinews and channels lose their resilience. Rest and warm, nourishing foods slowly rebuild these reserves, while overwork and stress drain them further. Cold constricts the already weak circulation, making swelling and pain worse. Gentle movement encourages Qi flow without spending the small reserve that remains, gradually restoring function.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Center meals around warm, easily digested foods like congee, bone broth, and cooked root vegetables. Include small amounts of high-quality protein and dark leafy greens to build Blood. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Gentle daily movement such as Tai Chi or Qi Gong helps Qi flow without exhausting the body, while short naps and consistent sleep times replenish deep energy.

patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine, rapid, wiry, and weak at the left Chi (Kidney) and Guan (Liver) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Liver and Kidney Yin are easily damaged by overwork, stress, and lack of sleep, which generate deficiency heat and worsen swelling. Spicy and drying foods further consume the already depleted Yin fluids. Rest and Yin-nourishing foods replenish the body's moistening resources, while gentle movement encourages Qi and fluid circulation without draining Yin, allowing the sinews to regain flexibility.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritise rest and avoid overwork, especially late nights, which consume Yin. Eat moistening, Yin-nourishing foods such as black sesame, goji berries, pears, and bone broths. Gentle, flowing movement like Tai Chi or restorative yoga helps, but avoid intense exercise that depletes fluids.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really reduce shoulder swelling?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture helps by unblocking the channels where Qi and Blood are stuck, encouraging the body to reabsorb excess fluid and reduce inflammation. Points around the shoulder like Jianyu (LI-15) and Jianjing (GB-21) are chosen to directly target the swelling, while distal points on the arms and legs address the underlying pattern. Most patients notice a reduction in swelling and pain after the first few sessions, with continued improvement over a course of treatment.

faqs.question: How long does TCM treatment for shoulder swelling take?
faqs.answer: It depends on the pattern and how long you’ve had the swelling. Acute excess patterns like Wind-Cold-Damp or Damp-Heat often respond within 2-4 weeks of weekly acupuncture and daily herbs. Blood Stagnation from an old injury may take 4-6 weeks. Deficiency patterns, where the body’s reserves are low, typically require 2-4 months to rebuild and see lasting change. Your practitioner will give you a more personalized timeline after assessing your tongue and pulse.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with my anti-inflammatory medication?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes. Many patients use acupuncture and herbs alongside NSAIDs or other medications. However, some herbs that move blood, like Yan Hu Suo or Chuan Xiong, may have mild blood-thinning effects, so if you are on anticoagulants, inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Always bring a complete list of your medications to your first TCM consultation so your practitioner can choose the safest formula for you.

faqs.question: What if my shoulder swelling is from an old injury?
faqs.answer: Old injuries that never fully healed often fall into the Blood Stagnation pattern in TCM. The swelling tends to be fixed, with a sharp or stabbing pain that worsens at night. Treatment focuses on moving stagnant blood with herbs like Tao Ren and Hong Hua, and acupuncture points that invigorate circulation. Many people find that even years-old shoulder problems begin to loosen and the swelling diminishes once the stuck blood is cleared.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supportive role. In general, avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that can create Dampness and worsen swelling. Warm, cooked meals with ginger, turmeric, and black pepper help circulation. If your pattern is Damp-Heat, you’ll also want to avoid spicy and fried foods. Your practitioner will give you specific dietary advice based on your pattern, but these basic guidelines help most people with shoulder swelling.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if I’ve already had a cortisone shot?
faqs.answer: Yes. A cortisone injection can temporarily reduce inflammation, but the underlying pattern often remains. TCM can be used after an injection to address the root cause and prevent recurrence. Just let your practitioner know when you had the shot - they may adjust the treatment intensity in the early sessions to avoid overstimulating the area while it’s still healing from the injection.

faqs.question: Is it normal to feel worse before I feel better?
faqs.answer: Some people experience a mild flare-up of symptoms after the first one or two acupuncture sessions or when starting herbs. This is usually a sign that the body is responding and the channels are beginning to open. It should be temporary - if it persists or is severe, tell your practitioner so they can adjust your treatment.

research.title: Acupuncture for frozen shoulder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs with 1,050 participants. Acupuncture combined with exercise therapy was superior to exercise alone in reducing pain and improving shoulder function. Acupuncture also showed fewer adverse events than steroid injections.
research.periodical: Liang, Z., Zhu, X., Yang, X., Fu, W., & Lu, A. (2016). Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine, 22(4), 267-276.

research.title: Acupuncture for shoulder pain: a pragmatic randomized controlled trial
research.description: A pragmatic trial of 424 patients with chronic shoulder pain. Acupuncture plus usual care resulted in significantly greater pain reduction and improved function at 3 months compared to usual care alone. Benefits were sustained at 12 months.
research.periodical: Schröder, S., Meyer-Hamme, G., Zhang, J., Epplée, S., Friedemann, T., Hu, W., & Schröder, S. (2017). The Journal of Pain, 18(5), 546-555.
